SALT AND STATIC — working notes, v0.3

Rough dump. Will tidy later.

## What this is

Grimdark horror, hard-ish sci-fi. A derelict-salvage crew story where the horror is
economic before it is biological. Nobody is a hero. The ship is a debt instrument with
people inside it.

Tone I'm after: cold, procedural, funny in a bleak way. The reader should never be told
who to root for.

## The setup

Deep salvage in the Kepler Drift. Corporations don't own ships, they own *routes* — a
crew leases a hull against future tonnage and the lease compounds while they sleep.

Reclamation law says a derelict belongs to whoever restores atmosphere to it first.
So the job is: get in, get the air on, get out before someone else does.

The thing nobody says out loud is that a derelict with atmosphere already restored is
worth nothing. Which means every crew that finds one has a reason to vent it again.

## Crew

**Odile Marchetti** — salvage master, forty years in. Reads a hull the way other people
read a room. Owns 3% of the lease, which is 3% more than anyone else aboard. Drinks to
keep her hands still, not to feel better. Her flaw is that she has never once been
wrong in a way that cost her, so she has no instinct for it.

**Teodor "Ash" Aszkiewicz** — pressure tech. Twenty-six. Signed a fifteen-year
indenture at nineteen and has done the arithmetic often enough to know he will not
outlive it. Competent, quiet, and looking for a door. He is the one who will do the
unforgivable thing, and the story should make you understand why.

**Ruth Okonjo-Vance** — the company's man, though she'd say auditor. She is not a
villain and it matters that she isn't. Her job is to make sure the numbers are true.
The numbers are true. That's the problem.

**The Passenger** — whatever they bring back. Not a monster in the costume sense. It
does not want anything. It metabolises. The horror is that it is not interested in them.

Odile and Ruth have history — a hearing, eleven years ago, that went Ruth's way.
Ash trusts Odile completely, which is the load-bearing mistake.

## How the bad thing works

Not a virus. A metabolic substrate. It reads pressure differentials and grows toward
them, which means it moves toward anywhere people are breathing.

Rules I want to keep honest:
- It cannot cross a hard vacuum gap. Ever. This is the only thing that reliably stops it.
- It does not think. It has no plan. If it seems to be hunting you, that is a pressure
  gradient and your own pattern-matching.
- Cutting it works. Cutting it is also how it gets into the air handling.
- It is slow. Everything bad that happens is because someone was in a hurry.

## Things I track per character

I want to be able to say, at any chapter, roughly where everyone sits:

    LEV — leverage over the others   0 to 100, moves when information changes hands
    DEBT — what they owe the lease   only goes up, never down
    AIR — literal remaining air      the one that makes everything else urgent
    COMP — how much they still act like a person   starts high, drops, never recovers

LEV and COMP are the interesting pair. COMP dropping should never be a surprise; the
reader should see the exact moment someone spends it.

DEBT does not move with rank or competence. A better salvager just owes faster.

## Shape of it

Opens with a clean job. Genuinely clean — I want the reader to relax. They restore
atmosphere on a small derelict, it goes fine, they get paid, the lease compounds anyway
and they are further behind than when they started. That's the hook: competence doesn't
help.

Then the big derelict. The *Verity Grange*, forty years dark, and someone has already
restored atmosphere to part of it. So somebody is aboard, or was.

Middle is the crew realising the salvage is worthless and the only asset is the thing
living in it. Ruth's audit is what makes that legible. She isn't wrong.

The turn is Ash venting a section with Odile still in it, and being right to.

I don't have an ending. I have two and I don't like either.

## How I want it written

- No omniscient narrator. Ever. If the reader knows it, someone aboard knows it.
- Never describe the substrate from outside. Only what a person with a torch sees.
- Don't explain the economics twice. Once, early, in dialogue, then never again.
- Avoid the word "creature".
- Chapters end on a decision, not on a reveal.
- If a scene's only job is to convey information, cut it and put the information in an
  argument instead.

## Still open

- Does Ruth survive? I go back and forth. She's more useful alive and more honest dead.
- Is the Passenger ever shown whole? Leaning no.
- Whether the lease is legally enforceable at all. If it isn't, the whole thing is a
  story about people who never checked. That might be better.
- Name of the corporation. Placeholder is "Hallix" and I hate it.
- Do I want a second derelict in act two or is that one derelict too many?
